passages.original: quam Graeci ἐτυμολογίαν appellant, id est verbum ex verbo veriloquium; nos autem novitatem verbi non satis apti fugientes genus hoc notationem appellamus, quia sunt verba rerum notae. Itaque hoc quidem Aristoteles σύμβολον appellat, quod Latine est nota. Sed cum intellegitur quid significetur, minus laborandum est de nomine.
passages.english: which the Greeks call *etymologia* (etymology), that is, word for word, "true-speaking"; but we, avoiding the novelty of a word not apt enough, call this kind *notatio* ("notation"), because words are tokens (*notae*) of things. And so Aristotle calls this a *symbolon*, which in Latin is *nota*. But when what is meant is understood, there is less need to labour over the name.
passages.notes: *Veriloquium* is Cicero's literal calque of Greek *etymologia* ("true speech"); rendered "true-speaking".

passages.original: nam id caderet in divisionem, quae talis est: Postliminio redeunt haec: homo navis mulus clitellarius equus equa quae frenos recipere solet—; sed cum ipsius postlimini vis quaeritur et verbum ipsum notatur; in quo Servius noster, ut opinor, nihil putat esse notandum nisi post, et liminium illud productionem esse verbi vult, ut in finitimo legitimo aeditimo non plus inesse timum quam in meditullio tullium; Scaevola autem
passages.english: For that would fall under division, which runs as follows: these return by *postliminium* [right of return]: a man, a ship, a pack-mule, a horse, a mare that is accustomed to take the bridle. But [it is a matter of etymology] when the force of *postliminium* itself is sought and the word itself is analysed. On this point our friend Servius, I believe, thinks that nothing is to be analysed except *post*, and holds that *-liminium* is merely an extension of the word, just as in *finitimus*, *legitimus*, *aeditimus* there is no more meaning in *-timus* than there is in *-tullium* in *meditullium*. Scaevola, however,
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence at "Scaevola autem", and the text supplies no following context. The bracketed "[it is a matter of etymology]" supplies the contrast implied by "sed cum": the case is one for *notatio* (etymology), set against the preceding division. *Postliminium* is the Roman legal right by which persons and certain property captured by the enemy recover their former status on return; it is kept as a Latin technical term. The Latin words *finitimus* (neighbouring), *legitimus* (lawful), *aeditimus* (temple-keeper) and *meditullium* (the middle) are cited as words, so they are left untranslated.

passages.original: ex hoc illa rhetorum ex contrariis conclusa, quae ipsi ἐνθυμήματα appellant; non quod omnis sententia proprio nomine ἐνθύμημα non dicatur, sed, ut Homerus propter excellentiam commune poetarum nomen efficit apud Graecos suum, sic, cum omnis sententia ἐνθύμημα dicatur, quia videtur ea quae ex contrariis conficitur acutissima, sola proprie nomen commune possedit.
passages.english: from this [come] those arguments of the rhetoricians concluded from contraries, which they themselves call *enthymēmata* (enthymemes); not that every thought is not called by its proper name an *enthymēma*, but, just as Homer, because of his excellence, made the common name of poets his own among the Greeks, so, although every thought is called an *enthymēma*, because the one which is constructed from contraries seems the sharpest, it alone has properly come to possess the common name.
passages.notes: The Homer comparison: among the Greeks "the poet" meant Homer.

passages.original: Opinio est autem non modo eos virtutem habere qui habeant, sed eos etiam qui habere videantur. Itaque quos ingenio, quos studio, quos doctrina praeditos vident quorumque vitam constantem et probatam, ut Catonis Laeli Scipionis aliorumque plurium, rentur eos esse qualis se ipsi velint; nec solum eos censent esse talis qui in honoribus populi reque publica versantur, sed et oratores et philosophos et poetas et historicos, ex quorum et dictis et scriptis saepe auctoritas petitur ad faciendam fidem.
passages.english: Now, the opinion [of virtue] attaches not only to those who have virtue, but also to those who seem to have it. And so those whom they see endowed with talent, with application, with learning, and whose life [they see to be] consistent and approved, like that of Cato, Laelius, Scipio and very many others, they suppose to be such as they themselves would wish [to be]; and they judge to be such not only those who are engaged in the offices bestowed by the people and in public affairs, but also orators and philosophers and poets and historians, from whose sayings and writings authority is often sought to create belief.
passages.notes: "qualis se ipsi velint" is ambiguous: either "such as they themselves would wish to be" (the observers) or "such as those men would wish themselves [to be thought]".
